title: The 1-3-6 benchmarks
text: The Joint Committee on Infant Hearing recommends screening by 1 month of age, confirmatory diagnostic evaluation by 3 months for those who do not pass, and enrolment in early intervention by 6 months for confirmed hearing loss. Meeting these ages gives the best speech, language and development outcomes.
source: Joint Committee on Infant Hearing. Year 2019 position statement. J Early Hear Detect Interv 4(2):1–44

title: Risk factors need later monitoring
text: Some babies pass the newborn screen but have risk factors for later or progressive hearing loss — family history, NICU care, CMV, hyperbilirubinaemia, ototoxic drugs, syndromes. JCIH advises at least one audiological review by about 9 months, or sooner if there is concern.
source: Joint Committee on Infant Hearing. Year 2019 position statement

title: OAE and AABR screening
text: Newborn screening uses otoacoustic emissions (OAE) or automatic auditory brainstem response (AABR). A “refer” means further testing is needed, not that the baby is deaf — many pass on rescreen. Babies with NICU stays should have AABR so that auditory neuropathy is not missed.
source: Joint Committee on Infant Hearing; WHO newborn and infant hearing screening

title: Why early matters for language
text: Children identified and supported by 6 months develop language on a par with hearing peers far more often than those identified later. The first months are a sensitive period for building the brain's hearing and language pathways, so delay is costly.
source: Yoshinaga-Itano C, et al. Language of early- and later-identified children with hearing loss. Pediatrics 102(5):1161–1171

title: Loss to follow-up is the main failure
text: The biggest weakness of screening programmes is babies who refer but never return for diagnosis or intervention. Clear tracking, reminders in the family's own language, and naming a responsible person for each baby are what keep babies in the 1-3-6 pathway.
source: CDC EHDI programme; WHO newborn and infant hearing screening
